documents.title: Generative AI in the Classroom
documents.summary: Teaching-center guide applying the Student Code of Conduct to AI: unauthorized or uncited AI use is an integrity violation, detectors are not recommended, and instructors get assignment-design ideas to discourage or incorporate AI. It also points to syllabus language and consultation.
documents.stance_why: The page states the integrity policy "already prohibits the use of unauthorized resources, including AI content generators" and treats unauthorized AI as unauthorized assistance or uncited plagiarism, so AI is off unless the instructor authorizes it. A coded restrict and B coded delegates; the page also suggests many ways instructors may integrate AI and sets no tiers, but its governing statement is a default ban conditional on authorization, so restrict.

units.why: The page's headline conclusion says the integrity policy covers AI: "already prohibits the use of unauthorized resources, including AI content generators". It binds students and fits P36 (AI as an unauthorized resource handled under integrity rules) better than P01 because the ban is conditional on authorization.
units.anchor: academic integrity policy already prohibits the use of unauthorized resources, including AI content generators
units.frag_start: Illinois State’s academic integrity policy already

units.why: The Center says it "updated the suggested academic integrity syllabus statement to note this fact specifically". This is a fact about how expectations are communicated through the syllabus, so P09 as the nearest type (it is a suggested statement, not a mandate, hence informs); admin because the Center acts, course-start because the topic is syllabus expectations.
units.resolution_why: A coded P09 / course-start; B coded UNCOVERED / before-course because P09 covers a required statement. The source only says the Center updated a suggested statement. P09 is the closest type and the syllabus is where expectations are communicated, so P09 / course-start with informs; an uncovered note is not warranted for a loose but real fit.
units.anchor: the Center has updated the suggested academic integrity syllabus statement to note this fact specifically
units.policy: The Center has updated its suggested academic integrity syllabus statement to note that the academic integrity policy prohibits unauthorized resources including AI content generators.

units.why: Detection is described as unsolved: "There is not yet a detection service that can definitively determine" authorship. This is a factual statement that detectors cannot be relied on, so P39, informing instructors.
units.anchor: There is not yet a detection service that can definitively determine whether content was produced
units.frag_start: There is not yet a detection
units.frag_end: are still in the early stages of development

units.why: Instructors are told they "should never put their students’ work into services that claim to be able to detect" AI, citing privacy and IP. P50 (protect personal data) fits better than P39 because the stated reason is privacy and consent. Modality is should-not ('should never').
units.resolution_why: Both coded P50, instructor, when-misuse. A said should-not, B said must-not. The source says instructors "should never put their students’ work into" such services "without their students’ informed consent", which is should-not, not must-not.

units.frag_start: Due to concerns about student privacy
units.policy: Instructors should never put their students’ work into AI-detection services or into generative AI services without their students’ informed consent.

units.why: CIPD 'cannot recommend' use of AI detectors because none has been vetted by peer-reviewed study: detectors should not be relied on, P39.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on every code. A anchored the "not aware of any ... vetted" clause with policy null; B anchored "we cannot recommend their use". The recommendation is the load-bearing part, so the anchor is B's and the policy is normalized to carry both halves of the sentence.

units.frag_start: Due to concerns about student privacy
units.frag_end: so we cannot recommend their use
units.policy: CIPD cannot recommend the use of AI detection services, because it is not aware of any that has been vetted through a published, peer-reviewed study.

units.why: The guide suggests a "style mismatch between two sections" as a sign of AI use. This is an evidence cue for identifying misuse, so P40.

units.why: Instructors can use Crossref to "verify a student’s sources"; many unknowns "may be a sign" of AI. A tool-based check to identify misuse, so P40.
units.resolution_why: Both coders said may. The source says only that unknown sources "may be a sign of an AI-generated paper", a statement of evidence like the style-mismatch sentence both coded informs, not a permission. Actor, phase and type are as coded.

units.why: Guidance says the Student Code of Conduct covers "unauthorized use of any resource or service not authorized by or acknowledged to the instructor", which includes AI. This classifies unauthorized AI use as an integrity violation: P36.

The sentence defines what counts as an integrity violation (unauthorized resources, which covers AI); it does not describe responding to a suspected case, so general. The response process is the separate unit about following the usual process.

units.resolution_why: A coded P36, B coded P19. The passage says solving equations or developing code with AI "would be examples of unauthorized uses of assistance", which classifies those uses as misconduct under the integrity policy rather than banning AI-produced work outright. P36 fits; P19 would lose the dependence on instructor authorization.

units.resolution_why: Same type, actor, phase and modality. unit_stance: A restrict, B permit. The sentence makes uncited AI text a violation ("plagiarism if ... not cited"); it is a condition on use rather than a grant, and instructor authorization still applies, so restrict.

units.why: Instructors with suspicions "should follow the same process you would during any other academic integrity concern". A procedure for suspected misuse via integrity processes: P36.

units.policy: Instructors who suspect AI-generated work should follow the same process as for any other academic integrity concern, as laid out by Student Conduct and Community Responsibilities.

units.why: Says the suggested academic integrity language 'can be added to your course syllabus and discussed with your students'; an optional (may) syllabus communication, P09 as nearest fit, though it does not require a statement.
units.resolution_why: A coded should, B coded may. The source says the language "can be added to your course syllabus", which is optional, so may. P09 is a loose fit because the Center suggests rather than requires a statement; it remains the nearest type.

units.why: Suggests using AI-generated content 'for student critique and discussion', teaching students to evaluate AI output: P44 (courses demonstrate AI use) fits better than P35 as AI is used as course material.

The course demonstrates AI output to students and has them evaluate it, which P44 covers ("courses teach or demonstrate AI use"); P35 fits less well because no assignment structure is changed.

One passage, one rule. P16 concerns AI-generated code under conditions, which this is not. The instructor imperative is should; P44 fits as the course uses AI draft content for teaching.

documents.title: Ethical Use of Generative AI (thesis, dissertation, capstone, comprehensive exams)
documents.summary: Graduate School statement on generative AI in culminating work. It requires disclosure to the committee and citation, ties unauthorized use to Policy 1.8, and lets units add rules.
documents.stance_why: The statement says AI "can support innovative and creative scholarship when used within appropriate guidelines" and then requires disclosure to the committee and citation, so AI is permitted with conditions.

units.why: Says generative AI 'can support innovative and creative scholarship when used within appropriate guidelines, which may vary by discipline': a conditional permission for thesis work, P62 (research/scholarship), not P02 since it is not a general default.
units.resolution_why: A coded P02, B coded P62. The sentence is a conditional permission ("can support innovative and creative scholarship when used within appropriate guidelines") scoped to thesis, dissertation, capstone and comprehensive-exam work, which is the scholarship type P62; P02 is a general default and this document governs only graduate culminating work.
units.anchor: can support innovative and creative scholarship when used within appropriate guidelines

units.why: "All use of generative AI ... must be disclosed to the student’s committee by the student" is an explicit disclosure requirement: P24.
units.anchor: All use of generative AI in the thesis/dissertation/capstone/comprehensive exam process must be disclosed
units.frag_end: disclosed to the student’s committee by the student

units.why: Transparency "is required between the student, their committee and school/department" and the audience of the completed work; a broader disclosure duty to audiences, still P24.

units.policy: Transparency around the usage of generative AI is required between the student, their committee and school/department, and between the student and the audience of the completed thesis, dissertation, capstone and/or comprehensive exams.

notes: Reconciled from coder A and coder B. School and computing layers none found; course layer deferred. One A-only unit dropped: the top-of-page sentence that invented or poorly cited references are the easiest evidence of AI content, a near-repeat of the Crossref/hallucination unit that both coders coded. CIPD syllabus-statement units use P09 as a loose fit (a suggested, not required, statement); no UNCOVERED units remained. CIPD stance is restrict (default ban conditional on instructor authorization); a delegates reading is arguable. Missed by both coders and not added: Graduate School sentence 'It is vital that students uphold the core principles of academic and research integrity'.
